name: Bare NP Construction

1.details: Refers to or predicates non-count substance/material

2.definition: Uses a bare plural for kind reference, classification, or an indefinite set
2.details: Bare plurals can receive a kind, generic, predicative, or episodic interpretation from the construction around them.

examples.note: Episodic use with a contextually supplied set of dogs

3.definition: Ascribes a role with a bare singular count NP
3.details: A licensed role NP can be bare as a predicative, in certain prepositional frames, or as an ascriptive supplement. The same role noun generally needs a determiner when used as an ordinary argument referring to the incumbent.

4.details: Refers to uniquely identifiable individual through proper name

5.details: Refers to or predicates generic activity type

examples.note: Activity reference (the adjectival modifier supports the noun analysis; bare "playing piano" is a gerund-participial clause, not an NP)

6.details: Refers to or predicates temporal point/period

examples.note: Articleless place name with a nominal head
Specifies a place by its name

8.details: Refers to or predicates abstract notion/quality

projection.target: A bare NP can be singular count in a restricted role or naming use, while bare plurals and non-count nouns can normally be arguments. Compare Lee became chair, Chair called on the name reading, and We bought chairs.
projection.evidence: CGEL provides independent distributional grounds for these kinds of bare uses. Absence of a determiner alone does not fix their interpretation.

relatedConstructions.notes: The NP consists of its nominal and has no overt determiner.
Dogs barked and Those dogs barked share the same nominal. The overt demonstrative in the second selects a contextually identifiable set.

curious.title: Noun phrases with no small word in front
curious.summary: Some noun phrases stand alone with no the, a or similar word, and still work as subjects, objects and names.
curious.body: Water is essential. Dogs are loyal. Monday works. Toronto was the next stop. None of these phrases has a small word like the or a in front of its noun, yet each is a complete phrase. Which meaning you get depends on the sentence around the phrase. Dogs are loyal talks about dogs as a kind, while Dogs barked all night is about a set of dogs the context supplies. Role words can go bare too: Lee stayed president. A word like chair needs something in front of it in other sentences, but in Jo became chair it can stand alone.
curious.try: Say Dogs are loyal and Those dogs barked. What does the extra word those change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain when a noun phrase can appear without a determiner and why the reading depends on the construction.
teacher.explain: A bare NP consists of a nominal with no overt determiner. The dictionary lists uses for non-count substances (Water is essential), bare plurals (Dogs are loyal; Those are bears; Dogs barked all night), proper names, activities, times, places and abstract concepts. A singular count noun can be bare only in restricted roles or naming uses (Lee stayed president, Jo became chair), whereas bare plurals and non-count nouns can normally be arguments. Not having a determiner doesn't fix the interpretation: kind, classification, or an episodic set all depend on the surrounding construction. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a determinerless NP or a bare noun phrase. Bare plural is the usual name for dogs with no determiner.

contrasts.note: Bare plural, with a set of dogs supplied by context.
Same nominal with an overt demonstrative, selecting a contextually identifiable set.

watch_for: A learner might think a missing determiner means the sentence is incomplete.
A learner might use the same bare noun for the incumbent of a role as an ordinary argument, though the dictionary notes that such a noun needs a determiner there.
A learner might read Dogs are loyal and Dogs barked all night as having the same kind of meaning.
teacher.activity: Give students a set of sentences with bare noun phrases (water, dogs, Monday, president). They sort them into kind, set, time, role and substance, and discuss how they decided.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Bare NP Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-bare-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).
